hints.junior: The new semantic search felt smarter but slower — every keystroke round-tripped to a server for a docs set of maybe 40 pages that rarely changed.
hints.mid: 400-700ms per query, paid on a corpus small and static enough that a one-time client-side load would have made queries after the first essentially free.
hints.staff: The mistake was defaulting to server-side without checking whether this corpus's size and change frequency actually justified a round trip per keystroke.

hints.junior: Type a search term in each mode — one waits on a network call every time, the other loads once and answers instantly after.
hints.mid: Broken mode simulates a real round trip per query. Fixed mode simulates one model load, then zero-network local search after.
hints.staff: The fixed mode's cost isn't gone, it moved earlier — compare the one-time load against the broken mode's cost repeating on every query.

hints.junior: Client-side downloads a model and the docs' vectors once, then searches locally. Server-side sends the query and waits for a round trip, every time.
hints.mid: Client-side pays a one-time cold start; server-side pays a per-query round trip — which wins depends on corpus size and search volume.
hints.staff: A third variable beyond size: change frequency. Client-side needs a re-shipped index on every content change; server-side re-indexes independently of any deploy.

hints.junior: This demo's corpus is eight documents on purpose — a client-side index at that size is nothing. Hundreds of pages changes the math.
hints.mid: No fixed page-count flips the answer — model size, searches per session, and whether the download can be prefetched all factor in.
hints.staff: A hybrid is legitimate: client-side index for the fixed core, server-side fallback for anything not yet baked into the shipped index.

sections.junior: Hey! This one's about a docs sidebar that got a smarter search feature and somehow got slower at the same time, because every single search had to round-trip to a server for a doc set that barely ever changed.

There are really two ways to run this kind of search. Ship the model to the browser and search locally after one upfront download, or send every query to a server and wait for a response each time. Which one wins depends on how big your content is and how often it changes.
Try searching the same small set of documents both ways. One mode makes a real network call on every search. The other loads once, up front, and then every search after that is instant.

For a small set of content that doesn't change much, doing search fully in the browser after one upfront load usually wins. For a big or fast-changing set, sending the query to a server usually wins. Pick based on your actual content, not on which one sounds more advanced.
